Both amounts are given, so find the **limiting reagent** first.
**Step 1 — moles of each gas.** At STP one mole of any gas occupies **22·4 litres**:
H₂ : 22·4 / 22·4 = **1 mol**
Cl₂ : 11·2 / 22·4 = **0·5 mol**
**Step 2 — the balanced equation.**
H₂ + Cl₂ ⟶ **2**HCl
The ratio is 1 : 1, so 1 mol of H₂ would need 1 mol of Cl₂ — but only **0·5 mol** is present.
So **chlorine is the limiting reagent** and hydrogen is in excess.
**Step 3 — product from the limiting reagent.** Each mole of Cl₂ gives **2** mol of HCl:
n(HCl) = 2 × 0·5 = **1 mol** ✓
**Step 4 — what is left.** 0·5 mol of H₂ is consumed, leaving **0·5 mol of H₂ unreacted** in
the vessel.
Two steps decide the answer and each has its own trap: forgetting that chlorine runs out
first gives 2 mol, the answer you would get from the hydrogen; and forgetting the **2** in
front of HCl gives 0·5 mol.
A useful check is on **mass**: 1 mol H₂ (2 g) and 0·5 mol Cl₂ (35·5 g) make 1 mol HCl (36·5 g)
plus 0·5 mol H₂ (1 g) left over — 37·5 g in, 37·5 g out ✓
∴ 1 mol of HCl.

Note: the printed key gives (d), 1·5 mol. With chlorine limiting at 0·5 mol and two HCl
formed per Cl₂, the yield is exactly 1 mol, so the key is wrong and has been corrected to (a).

**Step 1 — moles of CO₂.** At STP one mole occupies 22 400 cc:
n(CO₂) = 448 / 22 400 = **0·02 mol**
**Step 2 — moles of carbonate.** A divalent metal carbonate decomposes 1 : 1 —
MCO₃ ⟶ MO + CO₂
so n(MCO₃) = **0·02 mol**
**Step 3 — molar mass of the carbonate.**
M(MCO₃) = 2 / 0·02 = **100 g mol⁻¹**
**Step 4 — atomic mass of the metal.** The carbonate group CO₃ weighs 12 + 48 = **60**:
atomic mass of M = 100 − 60 = **40**
**Step 5 — equivalent mass.** This is the step the question is really asking about:
**equivalent mass = atomic mass ÷ valency**
The metal is **divalent**, so
equivalent mass = 40 / 2 = **20** ✓
The trap is stopping at step 4 and answering 40 — the **atomic** mass. The word 'divalent' in
the question is there precisely so the valency is known, and the question asks for the
**equivalent** mass, which is half of it.
An atomic mass of 40 with valency 2 identifies the metal as **calcium**, and CaCO₃ has molar
mass 100 ✓ — a satisfying confirmation that the arithmetic is right.
∴ 20.

Note: the printed key gives (a), 40. That is the atomic mass; dividing by the valency of 2
gives an equivalent mass of 20, so the key is wrong and has been corrected to (b).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|67|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The link between the three quantities is
**atomic mass = equivalent mass × valency**
so the work is in finding the valency of M from the formula of its oxide.
**Step 1 — valency from the formula MₓO_y.** Oxygen is always divalent, so the y oxygen atoms
carry **2y** units of negative valency in total. Those must be matched by the x atoms of M, so
total valency of M = 2y
valency of each M atom = **2y/x**
**Step 2 — substitute into the relation.**
atomic mass = E × (2y/x)
= **2E(y/x)** ✓
**Step 3 — check against a known oxide.** Take Fe₂O₃, so x = 2 and y = 3. Iron's equivalent
mass in this oxide is 18·67, so
atomic mass = 2 × 18·67 × (3/2) = **56** ✓ correct for iron
Try it on a simpler case too: MgO has x = y = 1, giving atomic mass = 2E — and magnesium's
equivalent mass is 12 while its atomic mass is 24 ✓
The distractors are the same symbols rearranged: E/y, y/E and E/2(x/y) all fail the Fe₂O₃
check, which is the quickest way to eliminate them without redoing the derivation.
∴ 2E(y/x).

Note: the printed key gives (d), y/E. That expression does not even have the dimensions of a
mass — the equivalent mass appears in the denominator — so the key is wrong and has been
corrected to (a).

The key words are **at constant volume**, and everything follows from them.
**Step 1 — the work done.** The only work considered here is pressure-volume work,
w = −P ΔV
At constant volume ΔV = 0, so
**W = 0** — the gas cannot expand, so it can do no work on its surroundings, and none is done
on it.
**Step 2 — apply the first law.**
ΔU = q + W
= 500 + 0
= **500 J**
So **q = ΔU = 500 J and W = 0** ✓ — option (b).
All the heat supplied goes into the internal energy of the gas, which is why the temperature
rises from 298 to 308 K.
Now the others:
(a) and (c) set **q = W = 500 J**, which would require the gas to expand; at constant volume
it cannot.
(d) sets **ΔU = 0**, which would mean the temperature does not change — but the question says
it rises by 10 K, and for an ideal gas U depends only on temperature.
This is precisely why a **bomb calorimeter**, which holds the volume fixed, measures ΔU
directly, while a reaction in an open flask at constant pressure measures ΔH instead.
∴ q = ΔU = 500 J, W = 0.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|9|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
**Molar** heat capacity is the heat needed to raise **one mole** by one kelvin, so the mass
must be converted to moles first.
**Step 1 — moles of aluminium.**
n = 54 / 27 = **2 mol**
**Step 2 — temperature change.**
ΔT = 50 − 30 = **20 °C = 20 K**
(A *difference* in Celsius equals the same difference in kelvin, so no conversion is needed
here — unlike an absolute temperature.)
**Step 3 — the heat required.**
q = n × C(molar) × ΔT
= 2 × 25 × 20
= **1000 J = 1·0 kJ** ✓
The two things to be careful about are using **moles** rather than grams — dividing 54 by 27
is the step the question is testing — and reading the capacity as **molar**, not specific.
Had it been the specific heat capacity, 25 J K⁻¹ g⁻¹, the answer would have been
54 × 25 × 20 = 27 kJ.
Option (a), 1·51 kJ, and (d), 2·5 kJ, come from mishandling the mole conversion; option (b),
0·5 kJ, from halving rather than doubling.
A sense check: 25 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ is close to the Dulong–Petit value of about 25 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ that
almost all solid metals share at room temperature, so the figure is a realistic one.
∴ 1·0 kJ.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|10|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Heat capacity is defined as
**C = q / ΔT**
the heat supplied divided by the resulting rise in temperature.
Now consider water **in equilibrium with ice**. That is water at its **melting point**, 0 °C,
with both phases present. Supply heat to such a mixture and the temperature **does not rise
at all**: every joule goes into melting more ice, as the latent heat of fusion, and the
mixture stays at 0 °C until the last of the ice has gone.
So in the defining expression,
q is finite and positive, but **ΔT = 0**
C = q / 0 = **infinity** ✓
The heat capacity is therefore infinite at a phase transition — the system will absorb any
amount of heat without changing temperature.
The same is true at the boiling point, and of any first-order phase change.
Option (a), zero, is the opposite error: it would mean the temperature rises without any heat
being supplied. Options (c) and (d) are finite values — 75·48 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ is in fact the
molar heat capacity of **liquid water alone**, away from any transition, and it is offered
here precisely to catch someone who misses the words 'in equilibrium with ice'.
This is why an ice bath is such a reliable thermostat: it holds 0 °C against any heat leak,
until the ice runs out.
∴ infinity.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|19|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
By **definition**, the standard enthalpy of formation of an **element in its standard state**
is **zero** — there is nothing to form it from. So the answer is whichever option is an
element in the form that is stable at 298 K and 1 bar.
**(b) Cl₂(g)** ✓ Chlorine is a **gas** at 298 K, so gaseous Cl₂ **is** its standard state.
ΔfH° = **0** by definition.
**(a) Br₂(g)** ✗ This is the trap. Bromine is an element, but at 298 K its standard state is
the **liquid**, not the gas. Br₂(**l**) has ΔfH° = 0, whereas Br₂(**g**) has
ΔfH° = **+30·9 kJ mol⁻¹** — the enthalpy of vaporisation.
**(c) H₂O(g)** ✗ A **compound**, formed from H₂ and O₂, with ΔfH° = −241·8 kJ mol⁻¹.
**(d) CH₄(g)** ✗ Also a **compound**, ΔfH° = −74·8 kJ mol⁻¹.
The single letter in brackets is doing all the work in this question. Bromine and chlorine
are both halogens and both appear as X₂, but one is a gas at room temperature and the other
a liquid, and only the stable form gets the zero.
The convention matters because it is what makes a table of formation enthalpies possible at
all: every compound's value is measured relative to the elements, which are all pegged at
zero.
∴ Cl₂(g).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|27|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The heat released is proportional to the moles of **water formed**, which is fixed by the
**limiting reagent**.
**Step 1 — moles of each reactant.**
HCl : 0·1 M × 0·500 L = **0·05 mol**
NaOH : 0·2 M × 0·200 L = **0·04 mol**
**Step 2 — identify the limiting reagent.** The neutralisation is 1 : 1,
HCl + NaOH ⟶ NaCl + H₂O
so 0·05 mol of acid would need 0·05 mol of base, but only **0·04 mol** is present.
**NaOH is limiting**, and only **0·04 mol** of water is formed. The remaining 0·01 mol of HCl
stays unreacted and contributes nothing.
**Step 3 — multiply by the enthalpy of neutralisation.** For a **strong** acid with a
**strong** base this is a constant, **−57·3 kJ mol⁻¹**, whatever the pair — because the only
reaction actually occurring is H⁺ + OH⁻ ⟶ H₂O.
heat evolved = 0·04 × 57·3 = **2·292 kJ** ✓
The trap is using the acid, which is present in greater amount, and getting 0·05 × 57·3 =
2·865 kJ — not offered, which is itself a hint that the limiting reagent matters.
The volumes must also be converted to **litres** before multiplying by the molarity; using
millilitres directly would inflate everything by a thousand.
∴ 2·292 kJ.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|28|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Bond enthalpies give the reaction enthalpy as
**ΔH° = (sum of bond energies of bonds broken) − (sum of bond energies of bonds formed)**
The sign convention follows from the physics: breaking bonds **costs** energy, making them
**releases** it.
**Step 1 — bonds broken (the reactants).**
H₂ ⟶ one **H–H** bond = 433
Br₂ ⟶ one **Br–Br** bond = 192
total in = **625 kJ**
**Step 2 — bonds formed (the products).**
2HBr ⟶ **two** H–Br bonds = 2 × 364 = **728 kJ**
**Step 3 — subtract.**
ΔH° = 625 − 728 = **−103 kJ** ✓
The reaction is **exothermic**, which is right: HBr is more stable than the separate
elements, and hydrogen burns in bromine vapour.
The two things that decide the answer are the **factor of 2** for HBr — forgetting it gives
625 − 364 = +261 kJ, which is option (c), and the wrong sign as well — and the **direction of
the subtraction**. Broken minus formed, not the other way round; reversing it gives +103 kJ,
option (b).
A quick sanity check on the sign: more bond energy is released (728) than is spent (625), so
ΔH must be negative.
∴ −103 kJ.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|29|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Use ΔH = (bonds broken) − (bonds formed), and solve for the unknown O–H bond energy.
**Step 1 — count the bonds.** For
2H₂ + O₂ ⟶ 2H₂O
**broken:** 2 × (H–H) + 1 × (O=O) = 2(435) + 498 = 870 + 498 = **1368 kJ**
**formed:** each water molecule has **two** O–H bonds, and there are **two** molecules, so
**4** O–H bonds in all = 4x, where x is the average O–H bond energy
**Step 2 — set up the equation.**
ΔH = 1368 − 4x = **−571**
**Step 3 — solve.**
4x = 1368 + 571
4x = 1939
x = **484·75 ≈ 484 kJ mol⁻¹** ✓
The step that decides the answer is counting **four** O–H bonds, not two: each H₂O contains
two, and the equation produces two molecules. Using 2x instead would give 969·5, which is not
offered.
The **sign** is the other thing to watch. A bond energy is the energy **required** to break a
bond, so it is always **positive**; options (b) and (d), with negative values, can be
discarded on sight.
For comparison, the tabulated value for the O–H bond in water is about 463 kJ mol⁻¹; the
answer here is slightly higher because it is an average derived from this particular reaction
enthalpy.
∴ 484.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|37|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Two criteria for spontaneity are being compared, each appropriate to different conditions.
**The entropy criterion.** For an **isolated** system — constant volume V and constant
internal energy E, which is what the subscripts 'V, E' mean — the second law says the total
entropy must increase in any spontaneous (irreversible) change:
**(dS)V,E > 0** ✓
At equilibrium it would be zero; a negative value would mean the process runs backwards.
**The free-energy criterion.** For a system at **constant temperature and pressure** doing
only pressure-volume work, the condition becomes
**(dG)T,P < 0** ✓
Again, zero would mean equilibrium and positive would mean the reverse process is the
spontaneous one.
Both conditions together give option **(a)**.
The two are not independent: combining dG = dH − TdS with the second law shows that a
negative dG at constant T and P is exactly equivalent to a net entropy increase of system
plus surroundings. Gibbs energy is simply the more convenient bookkeeping, because it refers
only to the system.
Option (b), with both equal to zero, describes **equilibrium**, not an irreversible process.
Options (c) and (d) have one or both signs reversed, which would describe a change that
cannot happen spontaneously.
∴ (dS)V,E > 0, (dG)T,P < 0.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|39|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The link between the standard free energy change and the equilibrium constant is
**ΔG° = −RT ln K**
Rearranged,
ln K = −ΔG° / RT
Since R and T are both positive, the **sign of ln K is opposite to the sign of ΔG°**.
**If ΔG° < 0** (less than zero, as the question states), then
−ΔG°/RT is **positive**
so **ln K > 0**
and therefore **K > 1** ✓ — greater than unity.
So a reaction with a negative standard free energy change always has an equilibrium constant
greater than one, meaning the products predominate at equilibrium.
The three cases are worth holding together:
ΔG° **negative** ⇒ K **> 1**, products favoured
ΔG° **zero** ⇒ K **= 1**, neither side favoured
ΔG° **positive** ⇒ K **< 1**, reactants favoured
Option (d), zero, can be dismissed at once: K = 0 would require ln K = −∞ and so an
infinitely negative ΔG°, which no real reaction has.
It is worth adding that this says nothing about **rate**. A reaction may have a large K and a
strongly negative ΔG° and still not happen in a human lifetime without a catalyst — the
conversion of diamond to graphite being the standard example.
∴ greater than unity.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|41|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Start from
**ΔG° = −RT ln K**
and read off what K < 1 implies.
The logarithm of a number **less than 1** is **negative**:
K < 1 ⇒ ln K < 0
Substituting, with R and T both positive:
ΔG° = −RT × (a negative number) = **positive** ✓
So ΔG° is positive whenever K is less than unity.
What this means physically: a reaction with K < 1 settles with more reactant than product at
equilibrium, so starting from standard conditions — everything at unit concentration or
pressure — the reaction would actually run **backwards**. A positive ΔG° says exactly that:
the forward reaction is non-spontaneous under standard conditions.
The full picture:
K > 1 ⇒ ln K > 0 ⇒ ΔG° **negative**
K = 1 ⇒ ln K = 0 ⇒ ΔG° **zero**
K < 1 ⇒ ln K < 0 ⇒ ΔG° **positive** ✓
Option (b), zero, corresponds to K exactly 1, and option (c), negative, to K greater than 1 —
so the three numerical options map neatly onto the three cases, and only the sign has to be
worked out.
Option (a), '1·0', confuses the value of ΔG° with the value of K.
∴ positive.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|51|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Enthalpies of **combustion** can be combined by Hess's law to give an enthalpy of
**formation**. The formation reaction wanted is
6C(graphite) + 3H₂(g) ⟶ C₆H₆(l)
**Step 1 — write the combustion reactions.**
(i) C + O₂ ⟶ CO₂,  ΔH = −394
(ii) H₂ + ½O₂ ⟶ H₂O,  ΔH = −286
(iii) C₆H₆ + 7½O₂ ⟶ 6CO₂ + 3H₂O,  ΔH = −3270
**Step 2 — combine them.** Take 6 × (i) + 3 × (ii) − (iii). Reversing (iii) changes the sign
of its enthalpy, and the CO₂ and H₂O cancel, leaving exactly the formation equation.
**Step 3 — do the arithmetic.**
ΔfH = 6(−394) + 3(−286) − (−3270)
= −2364 − 858 + 3270
= **+48 kJ mol⁻¹** ✓
The general formula worth remembering is
ΔfH(compound) = Σ ΔcH(elements) − ΔcH(compound)
and the **minus sign in front of the compound's own combustion enthalpy** is the step most
often got wrong — adding it instead gives −6492.
The **positive** answer is itself informative: benzene is **endothermic** with respect to its
elements, so it is thermodynamically less stable than graphite and hydrogen. That it exists
at all is a matter of kinetics, not thermodynamics — and the same is true of acetylene, with
ΔfH = +227 kJ mol⁻¹.
∴ +48.
